diagnostic_evidence.quote: Second, since \Cref{GD} is a subgradient method, in general it is not a descent method.

The result of the theorem then immediately follows from this observation, \Cref{Quasi Remark}, the facts that $t_k\rightarrow 0$, and $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} t_k=\infty$, and Theorem 1 in \cite{kiwiel2001convergence}.

issues.failure_explanation: The cited Theorem 1 of Kiwiel yields only the liminf statement liminf_k κ(𝒟°(d_k)) = κ* — equivalently, the best-so-far values κ*_j (defined but unused in the theorem) satisfy κ*_j ↓ κ*. It gives no monotonicity of the raw sequence κ(𝒟°(d_k)). Projected subgradient steps with t_k → 0 and Σ t_k = ∞ are not descent steps — the paper itself states that GD "is not a descent method" — so the clause "κ(𝒟°(d_k)) ↓ κ*" asserts a monotone decrease the method does not guarantee and which can fail. The liminf claim itself is valid; only the "in particular" strengthening is wrong.

failure_location.quote: It then holds that $\underline{\lim}_{k \rightarrow \infty} \kappa(\cDo(d_k))=\kappa_{*}$; in particular, $\kappa(\cDo(d_k))\downarrow \kappa_{*}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace "in particular, κ(𝒟°(d_k)) ↓ κ*" with "equivalently, κ*_j ↓ κ*" (immediate from the liminf statement and the definition of κ*_j), or delete the clause.
issues.overall_effect: Only the monotone-convergence clause of thm:added-1 is unreliable. The asymptotic convergence guarantee (liminf = κ*), which justifies the GD algorithm and the abstract's "convergence guarantees", remains valid. No downstream formal result invokes monotonicity (the Nonasymptotic Theorem concerns the separate Subgrad V algorithm).
issues.title: Monotone-convergence clause in thm:added-1 is unsupported and generally false
issues.why_classification: The substantive guarantee (liminf convergence to κ*) is established and unaffected; the false clause is repaired by a one-line substitution using the already-defined κ*_j, requiring no new argument and harming no dependent result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: This follows from the equality conditions in the harmonic-arithmetic mean inequalities.

issues.failure_explanation: Under the paper's notion of ω-optimality for diagonal preconditioning (the identity scaling D = I is optimal for A), the correct characterization is eq:statomega: diag A = (tr A/n)e, i.e., all diagonal entries of A are equal — this is what the AM-GM equality condition on the diagonal entries A_ii d_i gives, and it is what the corollary's own proof sketch supports. The claimed equivalence with A = αI is false: A = [[1, 1/2],[1/2, 1]] is positive definite with equal diagonal entries, so D = I is ω-optimal for it, yet A is not a multiple of the identity and ∇ω(A) = (1/(n det(A)^{1/n}))(I − (tr A/n)A^{-1}) ≠ 0. Hence ∇ω(A) = 0 (equivalently A = αI) is strictly stronger than ω-optimality of the identity scaling; only the "if" direction holds.

failure_location.quote: The gradient $\nabla w(A)=0$ if, and only if, $A=\alpha I$ for some $\alpha >0$; i.e.,~$A$ is $\omega$-optimal if, and only if, it is a multiple of the identity.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the final clause with "i.e., the identity scaling is ω-optimal for A if and only if all diagonal entries of A are equal (diag A = (tr A/n)e)", as given by eq:statomega.
issues.overall_effect: The corollary's main claim — the Jacobi scaling D = α Diag(diag(A))^{-1} is ω-optimal — is correct and is what later results (block-diagonal corollary, numerics) use; only the final "i.e." characterization of when the identity is already ω-optimal is false. No dependent result relies on it.
issues.title: False 'if and only if' characterization of ω-optimality in cor:omegaoptDAD
issues.why_classification: A one-line correction of the characterization preserves the corollary's main claim (Jacobi optimality) and all its uses; no new lemma, construction, or guarantee is needed, and no substantive promise is lost.
